reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant epithelial dystrophy presenting in early childhood with myriad tiny intraepithelial cysts best seen on retroillumination
Caused by mutations in the cornea-specific keratin genes KRT12 or KRT3, which weaken the epithelial cytoskeleton
The cysts are most numerous in the interpalpebral zone and appear as fine clear vesicles extending toward the limbus
Many patients are asymptomatic, but cyst rupture can cause recurrent erosions with irritation, photophobia, and intermittent blurred vision
Vision is usually well preserved because the epithelium remains relatively transparent despite the cysts
Histology shows a thickened, fragile epithelium with intraepithelial cysts and a characteristic PAS-positive material (peculiar substance)
Management is conservative with lubrication and bandage contact lenses, reserving epithelial debridement or phototherapeutic keratectomy for troublesome erosions
Symptoms and cysts frequently recur after superficial treatment because the underlying keratin defect persists
reference.pathophysiology: Meesmann epithelial corneal dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the cornea-specific keratin genes KRT12 and KRT3. These keratins form the intermediate filament cytoskeleton of the corneal epithelium, and mutations weaken epithelial cell integrity. The fragile epithelium develops numerous small intraepithelial cysts containing degenerated cellular material, and the compromised cells are prone to breakdown. Cyst rupture and epithelial fragility give rise to recurrent surface disruption and irritation, while the overall epithelial transparency is largely maintained.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent corneal erosion syndrome of other cause
Punctate epithelial keratopathy from dry eye or toxicity
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with retroillumination to reveal intraepithelial cysts
Genetic testing for KRT12 and KRT3 mutations
In vivo confocal microscopy to visualise epithelial cysts
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the epithelial layer
Histology of debrided epithelium showing cysts and PAS-positive material
Fluorescein staining to document epithelial breakdown during symptomatic episodes
redFlags: Frequent painful erosions disrupting daily function
Non-healing epithelial defect raising concern for secondary infection
Unexpected stromal involvement or scarring suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Progressive visual loss that is atypical for this predominantly epithelial dystrophy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good, with vision usually well preserved. Recurrent erosions can cause chronic irritation, and symptoms tend to recur after superficial treatment because the underlying keratin defect is not corrected.
pitfalls: Mistaking the epithelial microcysts for contact-lens changes or viral keratitis
Expecting a permanent cure from epithelial debridement despite the genetic basis
Overtreating asymptomatic cysts that do not threaten vision
Failing to counsel about the autosomal dominant inheritance
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
